name: Dynamic programming for MDPs
positive_test: computes a value or policy by sweeping Bellman backups over a known transition model
negative_test: learning from sampled transitions without a given model
examples: policy iteration, value iteration, generalised policy iteration, asynchronous DP
notes: founder of the whole value-based lineage

name: Temporal-difference learning
positive_test: updates a value estimate toward a bootstrapped target built from the next state's own estimate
negative_test: updating toward a full Monte-Carlo return only
examples: TD(0), TD(lambda), true online TD, GTD

name: Off-policy TD control
positive_test: bootstraps from the max (or an argmax-decoupled estimate) over next-state actions
negative_test: bootstrapping from the action the behaviour policy actually took
examples: Q-learning, Double Q-learning, Expected SARSA(off-policy form)

name: On-policy TD control
positive_test: bootstraps from the action the current policy actually selects
negative_test: bootstrapping from a max over actions
examples: SARSA, Expected SARSA, n-step SARSA

name: Deep Q-networks
positive_test: fits Q-learning with a neural network plus a target network and a replay buffer
negative_test: tabular Q-learning; actor-critic with an explicit policy head
examples: DQN, Double DQN, Dueling DQN, NoisyNet-DQN, Rainbow, Ape-X, R2D2, Munchausen DQN
notes: the canonical "ancestor worth aggregating to"

name: Distributional value learning
positive_test: learns the full return distribution rather than only its expectation
negative_test: learning a scalar expected return
examples: C51, QR-DQN, IQN, FQF

name: Sample-efficient deep value learning
positive_test: raises updates-per-environment-step with explicit remedies for the resulting overfitting
negative_test: scaling data rather than updates
examples: DrQ, SPR, SR-SPR, BBF, REDQ
notes: SPR is multi-parent with self-predictive SSL

name: Policy-gradient methods
positive_test: differentiates expected return with respect to policy parameters via the score-function identity
negative_test: updating a value table or network with no explicit policy parameterisation
examples: REINFORCE, actor-critic, A3C, A2C

name: Actor-critic
positive_test: reduces policy-gradient variance with a learned value baseline or critic
negative_test: using an empirical return baseline only
examples: actor-critic, A3C, A2C, GAE, IMPALA/V-trace, ACER

name: Trust-region and clipped policy updates
positive_test: bounds the size of the policy change per update by a divergence or ratio constraint
negative_test: an unconstrained gradient step on the policy
examples: natural policy gradient, TRPO, PPO, PPO-clip, V-MPO

name: Group-relative policy optimisation
positive_test: replaces the learned critic with a baseline computed across a sampled group of completions
negative_test: using a learned value network as the baseline
examples: GRPO, RLOO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO
notes: the dominant recent RL-for-reasoning branch

name: Deterministic policy gradients
positive_test: backpropagates the critic's gradient through a deterministic actor
negative_test: sampling actions from a stochastic policy and using the score function
examples: DPG, DDPG, TD3, D4PG
notes: requires continuous actions

name: Maximum-entropy RL
positive_test: optimises return plus a policy-entropy term as part of the objective, not as a bonus
negative_test: entropy added only as an auxiliary regulariser with no soft-Bellman consistency
examples: soft Q-learning, SAC, MPO, soft actor-critic variants, REDQ

name: Model-based RL
characteristic: what the learned dynamics model is used for
positive_test: learns a transition or reward model and uses it to improve the policy or the value estimate
negative_test: learning a value or policy directly from environment samples only
examples: Dyna, PETS, Dreamer, MuZero

name: Model-generated experience
positive_test: uses the learned model to synthesise extra transitions for a model-free learner
negative_test: using the model only inside an action-selection search
examples: Dyna, Dyna-Q, MBPO, SLBO

name: Model-predictive control over a learned model
positive_test: re-plans an action sequence at each step by rolling the model forward
negative_test: amortising the plan into a policy network and never re-planning
examples: PILCO, PETS, CEM-MPC, MPPI, iCEM

name: Latent-dynamics world models
positive_test: learns dynamics in a compressed latent space and trains the policy inside it
negative_test: planning directly in observation space
examples: World Models, PlaNet, Dreamer, DreamerV2, DreamerV3, TD-MPC

name: Learned-model tree search
positive_test: combines a learned model with an explicit tree search that produces the acting policy
negative_test: planning by trajectory sampling without a tree
examples: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, MuZero, EfficientZero, Sampled MuZero
notes: the clearest case of one lineage spanning two roles

name: Offline reinforcement learning
characteristic: how the policy is kept inside the data's support
positive_test: learns a policy from a fixed logged dataset with no further environment interaction
negative_test: collecting new interaction at any point in training
examples: BCQ, CQL, IQL, Decision Transformer

name: Explicit policy constraint
positive_test: penalises or projects the learned policy toward the behaviour policy
negative_test: penalising the value function instead
examples: BCQ, BEAR, TD3+BC, BRAC

name: Pessimistic value penalty
positive_test: lowers values of out-of-distribution actions so they are never selected
negative_test: constraining the policy's action distribution directly
examples: CQL, COMBO, pessimistic MDPs, EDAC

name: Implicit and weighted-regression policy extraction
positive_test: extracts a policy by advantage-weighted regression without querying unseen actions
negative_test: computing a max over actions outside the data
examples: AWR, AWAC, IQL, XQL, SQL

name: Return-conditioned sequence modelling
positive_test: casts control as supervised next-token prediction conditioned on a desired return
negative_test: fitting a value function and improving a policy against it
examples: Decision Transformer, Trajectory Transformer, RvS, Multi-Game DT
notes: signal is a label, not a reward, despite being RL

name: Multi-agent RL
characteristic: how the joint value or joint policy is factored
positive_test: trains two or more interacting policies whose returns depend on each other
negative_test: a single agent in a stationary environment
examples: QMIX, MADDPG, MAPPO

name: Independent learners
positive_test: each agent runs a single-agent algorithm treating others as part of the environment
negative_test: any explicit factorisation of a joint value or a centralised critic
examples: IQL, IPPO, independent A2C

name: Value factorisation
positive_test: decomposes a joint action-value into per-agent terms under a monotonicity or additivity condition
negative_test: learning the joint value without any decomposition
examples: VDN, QMIX, QTRAN, QPLEX, Qatten

name: Centralised critic, decentralised actors
positive_test: trains a critic with access to global state while each actor sees only its own observation
negative_test: both training and execution use only local information
examples: MADDPG, MAPPO, COMA, FACMAC

name: Equilibrium-computing methods
positive_test: computes an approximate equilibrium rather than a best response to fixed others
negative_test: optimising against a frozen opponent
examples: fictitious play, CFR, Deep CFR, NFSP, Nash-Q, regret matching

name: Hierarchical RL
characteristic: what the temporal abstraction is defined over
positive_test: learns a policy over temporally extended sub-policies with their own termination
negative_test: a flat policy over primitive actions
examples: options framework, option-critic, FeUdal networks, HIRO, HAC

name: Bandit algorithms
characteristic: how uncertainty about arm values is turned into a choice
positive_test: selects among actions with immediate feedback and no state transition
negative_test: a setting with state dynamics and delayed credit
examples: UCB1, Thompson sampling, EXP3
notes: shares its characteristic with L.explore by design

name: Stochastic and contextual bandits
positive_test: assumes i.i.d. rewards per arm, possibly conditioned on a context vector
negative_test: an adversarial reward sequence
examples: UCB1, LinUCB, LinTS, Thompson sampling, KL-UCB

name: Adversarial bandits
positive_test: guarantees regret against an arbitrary, possibly adaptive reward sequence
negative_test: an i.i.d. reward assumption
examples: EXP3, EXP4, Tsallis-INF

name: Best-arm identification
positive_test: spends a fixed budget to identify the best arm, not to maximise cumulative reward
negative_test: minimising cumulative regret while acting
examples: successive halving, sequential halving, LUCB, racing
notes: had L.hpo.bandit as a second parent, which made a 2-cycle; the edge runs HPO -> BAI only

name: Off-policy evaluation and learning
positive_test: estimates the value of a policy from logs collected under a different policy
negative_test: evaluating a policy by running it
examples: inverse propensity scoring, self-normalised IPS, doubly robust OPE, FQE
notes: shares estimators with causal inference

name: Budget-allocation search
positive_test: reallocates compute across running trials by early-stopping the weak ones
negative_test: running every trial to completion
examples: successive halving, Hyperband, ASHA, BOHB, PBT

name: Controller-based search
positive_test: trains a controller policy that emits architectures, rewarded by their accuracy
negative_test: mutating a population or relaxing the space
examples: NASNet/Zoph-Le, ENAS, MetaQNN

name: Discrete optimisation inside learning
positive_test: solves a combinatorial subproblem as a step inside a learning procedure
negative_test: solving a continuous parameter optimisation
examples: Hungarian matching, Sinkhorn, Viterbi, beam search as search
notes: underrated: appears inside many deep pipelines

name: Assignment and matching
positive_test: solves a bipartite matching to pair predictions with targets or clusters
negative_test: sorting or thresholding heuristically
examples: Hungarian algorithm, DETR bipartite matching, auction algorithm

name: Optimal transport
positive_test: computes a coupling minimising transport cost between two distributions
negative_test: computing a pointwise divergence
examples: Sinkhorn-Knopp, entropic OT, Wasserstein distance, Gromov-Wasserstein, SwAV assignment step

name: Greedy submodular selection
positive_test: selects a set greedily under a submodular objective with an approximation guarantee
negative_test: selecting by independent per-item score
examples: facility location coresets, greedy maximum coverage, k-center greedy

name: Exact combinatorial solvers
positive_test: solves to optimality with branch and bound or an integer program
negative_test: using a heuristic with no optimality claim
examples: branch and bound, mixed-integer programming, constraint programming, SAT-based learning
